latin.2028: XXXIII. Atque ut viri illi Doctissimi mentem suam ea de re distinctius explicent, aiunt, Se considerare in objecto scientiae divinae duos status, possibilitatis & futuritionis, sed tria momenta. Primum, quando Deus intuendo suam omnipotentiam vidit quid absque contradictione a se fieri possit. Alterum, quando omnium fieri possibilium modos, connexiones, & concatenationes apud se decreto absoluto praefinivit, id est, quid causa, quid effectum, quid medium, quid finis, quid prius, quid simul, quid posterius foret, aut non foret; Sed cum hac cautione, si vellet eas futuras. Tertium, quando inter illas res, sub conditione tali praefinitas, discrimen statuit, relicta quibusdam conditione illa, & superaddito tali decreto, Nolo futuras, ab aliis sublata conditione, ejusque in locum substituto tali decreto, Volo futuras. In tertio momento, rem demum extrahi ex statu possibilitatis in statum futuritionis: in prioribus duobus manere in statu possibilitatis; hoc tamen discrimine, quod eas in primo per naturam, & ante omnem voluntatis actum cognoscat, in secundo post actum voluntatis. Quae sunt quoque eorum verba tertia illa sectione, num. 13. Ex quibus verbis patet eos futura contingentia sub conditione non habere pro vere futuris, sed pro mere possibilibus, & tamen velle ut eorum cognitio, non ad scientiam Dei naturalem, sed ad liberam pertineat.
latin.2029: XXXIV. Porro hanc suam doctrinam fatentur illi se sumpsisse a Samuele Retorforti Scoto, ex quo, ut certissimum fundamentum, ibidem supponunt: Quod voluntas Dei ad nulla entia, vel quae actu sunt, vel quae sunt in potentia, seu aliquando actuanda, seu in actum nunquam deducenda, sit indeterminata, dubia, aut suspensa, seu habens in se potentialitatem, suspensionem & privationem actus secundi, qualis reperitur in voluntate creata, sed quod sit per eminentiam sui actus, respectu omnis entis ab aeterno determinata. Unde colligunt, Deum necessario velle, vel non velle omnes concatenationes & connexiones entium possibiles, adeoque in omnibus propositionibus conditionatis de futuro contingenti, verum esse ex definita & certa Dei voluntate, quod si talis vel talis conditio poneretur, sequeretur hoc & non aliud.
latin.2030: XXXV. Et certe Retorfortis ille, nuper in Academia Andreapolitana, Theologiae Professor, Vir quoque Doctus & subtilis, eodem utens principio, affirmat Keilitas Davidem in manus Saulis tradituros, si apud eos permansisset, & Tyrios acturos poenitentiam, si signa vidissent, & alia ejusmodi, Deus cognovit scientia libera in decreto praedeterminante, quo concatenationem entium omnium possibilium absolute praedefinivit, quod certe, inquit, spectat ad admirandam Dei providentiam, cujus voluntas ad nulla entia, vel quae actu sunt, vel quae possibilia sunt, est indeterminata & suspensa. In Exercitationibus Apologeticis pro divina gratia, cap. 5. de scientia Media.
latin.2031: XXXVI. Alii vero existimant, multas aut innumeras potius propositiones de futuris contingentibus sub aliqua conditione fieri & fingi posse, quae sub scientiam divinam non cadunt, nec quicquam exprimunt quod ab ipso Deo sciri & cognosci possit, non quod Deum veritatem ullam ignorare, aut aliquid esse revera futurum quod Deus futurum non sciat, sed quoniam existimant propositiones istas nihil significare quod determinate verum vel falsum sit; & quae in eis futura sub certa conditione negantur, vel affirmantur, non esse magis futura, quam non futura, sed indifferentia ad utrumque.
latin.2032: XXXVII. Exempli causa, affirmat aliquis, quod si Deus mundum alium crearet, & certos Angelos in eo conderet, in his, aut illis circumstantiis, Angeli isti essent in officio suo & amore Dei perseveraturi. Ex eorum mente, id quod affirmatur in conditionali ista propositione neque verum, neque falsum est, ac proinde ut tale a Deo cognosci non potest; sed res est ex se mere possibilis, & quae indifferens est, ut ita sit, vel non sit; Eamque ita se habere novit Deus; ac proinde, si dicatur ista propositione nullam veritatem Deo scibilem contineri, omniscientiae divinae nihil propterea detrahitur.
latin.2033: XXXVIII. Etenim absurdam putant sententiam eorum qui infinita decreta Deo tribuunt de connexionibus contingentibus cujuscunque possibilis cum altero possibili, etiam in iis in quibus nullus ordo, subordinatio, aut cohaerentia apparet. Quasi Deus decrevisset quaecunque futura essent in infinitis mundis a se creabilibus, suppositis infinitis diversis conditionibus. Quae est sententia jamjam ex Samuele Retorforti, & Thesibus Voetii relata: quam expresse rejicit Strangius, Tractatu de Voluntate & Actionibus Dei circa peccatum, lib. 1. cap. 5. & lib. 3. cap. 13. Et Tuissus quoque in dissertatione de scientia Media, lib. 3. pag. 472.
latin.2034: XXXIX. Neque tamen negant omnem in Deo scientiam eorum quae essent, vel fuissent contingenter futura, sub aliqua conditione, quae nunquam posita est, nec etiam unquam ponenda. Agnoscunt enim ejusmodi quaedam in scriptura praedici, adeoque Deo nota & perspecta fuisse. Sed pertendunt istam scientiam non praecessisse liberum voluntatis divinae decretum. Non quod admittant in Deo decreta quaedam conditionata, quibus velit aliquid fieri sub conditione quae nunquam locum habitura est: aut etiam explicita & formalia decreta de connexione duorum eventuum quorum neutrum revera existet: sed quoniam ex absolutis quibusdam Dei decretis de rebus reapse futuris sequitur, posita tali, vel tali conditione, haec & illa futura fuisse.
latin.2035: XL. Exempli causa, noverat Deus Saulem venturum in urbem Kehilam, & Kehilanos Davidem Sauli tradituros, si David ea in urbe maneret: quia decreverat Davidem ex manibus Saulis eripere, non per miraculum aliquod, aut extraordinariam quandam animi mutationem sive in Saule, sive in Kehilanis, sed per Davidis recessum & fugam; Unde sequitur Davidem in manus Saulis fuisse tradendum si mansisset apud Kehilanos: quanquam explicitum ejusmodi decretum in Deo non ponamus, Volo ut Ceilani Davidem tradant si maneat apud ipsos.
latin.2036: XLI. Sic rem istam exponit Guil. Amesius in sua rescriptione ad Grevinchovii Responsum cap. 15. Dignum, inquit, & hoc accurata contemplatione: decretum Dei vel ut formale statutum & explicitum concipi, vel ut implicitum & virtuale, quod virtute alterius decreti includitur: implicitum vero tantum dari in futuris conditionatis contingentibus, quae nunquam existunt, quia virtute actuali decretis, hoc vel illo posito existerent. Decreverat Deus liberare Davidem a manibus virorum Ceilae mediante fuga, non mutatione animorum praeter ordinem. Ex hoc actuali fluit conditionatum illud contingens: si non fugiat David, tradetur. Et hoc sensu ait futurum conditionatum decreto libero inniti, adeoque per Visionis scientiam intelligi, quae non sit de iis tantum quae absolute futura sunt; sed & de iis quae ex actuali decreto jam facto fluerent, hac vel illa conditione posita.
latin.2037: XLII. Porro praecipuum fundamentum quo nituntur Tuissus, Retorfortis, Voetius, Amesius, & alii, dum negant in Deo dari cognitionem contingenter futurorum sub aliqua conditione, ante liberum ipsius decretum, illud est quod, ex eorum mente, Nihil futurum est priusquam decreverit Deus illud esse futurum. Unde sequitur, ante Dei decretum nihil ut futurum concipi atque cognosci posse. Nihil autem vel absolute vel conditionate futurum esse, priusquam decernat Deus illud esse futurum, inde probant, quod nulla causa fingi vel cogitari possit, per quam res ex possibili ab aeterno futura fiat, praeter Dei decretum. Cum enim nihil temporale causa possit esse ejus quod aeternum est, ad nihil eorum quae in tempore fiunt, futuritionis, quae est ab aeterno, causa referri debet, sed necesse est ut ista futuritio causam habeat aliquam aeternam, quae alia esse non potest quam liberum Dei decretum: ut millies repetit Tuissus in sua dissertatione de scientia Media.
latin.2038: XLIII. Voetius vero, seu apud ipsum Nathenus, postquam multis disputavit contra scientiam Mediam, sic tandem concludit, Ex iis quae hactenus contra scientiam mediam disputata sunt, manifestum est totam praesentis controversiae difficultatem recidere in hoc punctum: An futura conditionata libera, ex sua natura ad futuritionem & non futuritionem indifferentia, ab aeterno potuerint transiisse in statum rei futurae aliter quam per decretum divinum, quod causa sit omnis qualiscunque etiam futuritionis? Hoc est fundamentum fundamentorum, cui tota causae moles incumbit; hoc est postulatum illud quod & nos adversariis concedere, & ipsi nobis probare non possunt.
latin.2039: XLIV. Strangius vero qui non putat, cum modo dictis Theologis, cujuslibet eventus ab aeterno futuritionem non aliunde quam ex Dei libero decreto pendere, alio argumento, quod invictum esse existimat, probare contendit contingentia libera, ut futura non posse a Deo cognosci, ex ulla hypothesi, ex qua non necessario inferatur determinatio voluntatis creatae. Argumentum autem ejus tale est. Conditionata quorum consequens non habet necessariam connexionem cum antecedente non possunt certo sciri, ac proinde nec sunt scibilia a Deo, cujus scientia est certissima & omnino infallibilis. At ejusmodi sunt conditionata quae statuuntur esse objectum scientiae mediae, &c. Majorem probat, quia, inquit, Nisi objectum sit certo verum, certo cognosci non potest: quamdiu enim res est incerta, certo sciri non potest; nihil autem est certo verum quod non est necessario verum, necessario inquam vel absolute, vel ex hypothesi. Ac proinde conditionata scientia ut sit certa & infallibilis, oportet ut objectum ejus sit conditionata propositio necessaria: nulla autem conditionalis propositio est necessaria, in qua illatio non est necessaria. Tractatu de Voluntate Dei circa peccatum lib. 3. cap. 11.
latin.2040: XLV. Ut autem quid ipse quoque sentio paucis aperiam, Primo illud certum est &, ut patet ex dictis, ab omnibus concessum, Nihil esse sub ulla conditione libere futurum, & ut tale cognosci posse, nisi in conditione sub qua futurum dicitur, includatur Dei decretum de non denegando creaturae concursu ad agendum necessario. Nempe propositiones omnes de futuris conditionatis, ut verae esse possint, sic exponendae & intelligendae sunt; creatura haec, vel illa in tali rerum ordine constituta, hoc aut illud faciet; modo Deus velit cum ea concurrere, prout concurrere solet, & ut concurrat necesse est ad hoc ut creatura actionem suam elicere possit.
latin.2041: XLVI. Secundo, illud quoque concedendum existimo, propositiones omnes de futuris conditionatis liberis & contingentibus, in quibus ejusmodi conditio subintelligitur, determinate veras vel falsas esse. Saltem hoc negare non possunt Thomistae recentiores, & alii qui cum ipsis in hoc negotio sentiunt, & alioqui scientiam Mediam acerrime impugnant. Cum enim ad hoc ut creatura agat, ex eorum sententia, necesse sit Deum illam praemovere & praedeterminare, posita autem Dei praedeterminatione, necessario sequatur creaturae actio, juxta eorum hypotheses infallibilis & necessaria est haec conditionalis, Si Deus vellet talem creaturam in hoc, aut illo statu constituere, & nihil ad agendum necessarium ipsi denegare, hoc aut illud ageret: quandoquidem in illa conditione continetur decretum Dei de illa ad agendum praedeterminanda.
latin.2042: XLVII. Et certe quae rationes suadent absolutas propositiones de futuris contingentibus determinatam veritatem, vel falsitatem habere, in hisce conditionatis locum etiam habere videntur. Nempe quod fieri non potest, quin ex duabus contradictoriis, altera sit vera, altera falsa. Item quod in omni disjunctiva vera, una pars saltem debet esse vera. Nam haec disjunctiva vera est, Si Petrus in occasione tali constituatur, nec Deus ei solitum concursum suum deneget, peccabit, vel non peccabit. Et hae quoque duae sibi mutuo contradicunt, Petrus si in eo rerum ordine collocetur, nec Deus nolit cum eo ad agendum concurrere, hoc aget. Et Petrus si in eo rerum ordine collocetur, nec Deus nolit cum eo ad agendum concurrere, hoc non aget.
latin.2043: XLVIII. Quod si quis dicat nihil futurum esse, nisi dependenter a Dei decreto; & sic ante decretum Dei, rem non esse magis futuram quam non futuram, sed indifferentem ad hoc, ut futura vel non futura sit; adeoque neutrum de ea vere affirmari posse: Respondeo ad hoc, ut res absolute futura sit, praerequiri quidem quoddam Dei decretum, a quo pendeat ejus futuritio: sed ad hoc ut res non sit simpliciter futura, sed tantum futura esset sub aliqua conditione, non requiri decretum quod actu in Deo sit; sed sufficere decretum quod, juxta hypothesin, in Deo ponendum esset.
latin.2044: XLIX. Praeterea certum est, & ab omnibus concessum, nullam omnino veritatem qualiscunque sit fugere intellectum divinum: ac proinde cum propositiones de libere futuris, sub conditione saepius exposita, determinatam veritatem habeant, sunt illae quoque divinae scientiae objectum. Adeoque novit Deus quid singulae creaturae possibiles facturae essent, si vellet illas in hoc aut illo statu condere, nec eis quicquam negare eorum quae ad agendum necessaria sunt.
latin.2045: L. Hanc etiam propositionem, quae ex praecedenti sequitur, negare non possunt illi qui sine Dei concursu praevio & praedeterminante, nullam a creaturis actionem edi posse putant. Manifestum est enim, fieri non posse quin Deus cognoscat, quid acturae essent singulae creaturae possibiles, si vellet eas non tantum creare, sed etiam ad agendum applicare & praedeterminare. Istud fatetur Tuissus, qui postquam observavit Suarezium docere propositiones conditionatas de futuris contingentibus, quae sunt objectum scientiae divinae, includere in antecedente voluntatem divinam, scilicet, si ipsa velit talem effectum, vel saltem velit illum permittere, & ad illum concurrere, subjungit, Juxta hunc sensum concedimus conditionales illas obtinere quas fingunt Jesuitae. Dissertatione de scientia Media, lib. 3. pag. 465.
latin.2046: LI. Nec minus evidens est, juxta eorundem Doctorum principia, scientiam illam qua Deus cognoscit quid creatura quaelibet possibilis actura esset in hoc aut illo rerum statu, si Deus illi concursum ad agendum necessarium subministrare vellet, in Deo locum habere ratione priusquam de rebus quicquam decreverit. Etenim priusquam concipiamus Deum aliquid decernere, verum est, quod si Deus creaturam aliquam vellet concursu suo ad agendum movere & praedeterminare, ageret proculdubio id ad quod moveretur & determinaretur. Nec veritas hujus propositionis ab aliquo Dei decreto antecedente pendet, quo decreta sit connexio possibilis illius decreti cum eventu qui ex illo sequeretur.
latin.2047: LII. Imo etiam plane commentitium, neque tantum sapientiae, sed etiam divinae bonitati repugnans videtur illud decretum quo nonnulli volunt, ut supra retulimus, Deum omnium fieri possibilium connexiones & concatenationes apud se praefinivisse, priusquam decerneret aliquid esse futurum. Nam si ita esset, oporteret ut Deus, antequam hunc mundum creare statueret, hujusmodi decreta apud se concepisset, si velim Adamum creare, volo ut ejus lapsus cum ejus tentatione necessario cohaereat. Si velim creare Davidem & illum videre Bathscebah, volo ut cum isto visu connexa sit istius mulieris concupiscentia. Item, volo ut tales occasiones peccandi consequantur talia peccata, si decernam tales occasiones fore. Imo volo ut in infinitis mundis a me creabilibus hi & illi eventus contingenter possibiles cum his & illis ejusdem naturae eventibus nexum habeant inseparabilem. Quae certe decreta non tantum plane otiosa, frivola & frustranea sunt, sed maxime dedecent bonitatem & justitiam illius qui Deus nolens iniquitatem est.
latin.2048: LIII. Negari ergo cum aliqua ratione non potest, & debet ab omnibus concedi, dari in Deo scientiam quandam eorum quae libere & contingenter futura sunt, sub certa conditione, antequam ullum actuale de rebus futuris decretum in Deo concipiamus. Tota difficultas est An conditio sub qua res futura dicitur, includere debeat decretum de causa secunda ad agendum praemovenda ac praedeterminanda, an vero sufficiat ut decretum, quod juxta conditionem illam in Deo ponendum esset, sit solum de praebendo concursu quodam ex se indifferenti, & qui a causa secunda ad certam actionis speciem determinetur.
latin.2049: LIV. Omnes illi Theologi qui sine concursu Dei causam secundam ad agendum applicante & praedeterminante nihil fieri existimant, pertendunt nullam propositionem de futuris contingentibus & conditionatis veritatem aliquam habere, adeoque ut veram esse cognoscibilem, nisi in conditione supponatur decretum de agente libero praemovendo & praedeterminando. Volunt enim actionis cujuscunque futuritionem a tali decreto pendere, imo juxta nonnullos, tanquam a causa unica atque solitaria, & sine tali decreto nullam causae secundae actionem futuram esse posse. Verum in ea sumus sententia causas secundas multa in tempore agere ad quae a Deo non praedeterminantur. Nec enim videmus quomodo Deus autor peccati non esset, si praedeterminaret causas liberas ad actus per se vitiosos & intrinsece malos, verbi causa ad blasphemiam, & ad Dei odium. Si autem actio aliqua causae liberae esse potest sine Dei praemotione & praedeterminatione, ad hoc ut actio aliqua futura sit, vel futura esset, non necesse est poni, vel supponi in Deo decretum de creatura ad agendum praemovenda & praedeterminanda: sed sufficit decretum de eo concursu praebendo, sine quo creatura nihil agere potest, & qui ad ejus actionem revera necessarius est.
latin.2050: LV. Praesertim vero illud nullo modo probare possum quod Gul. Tuissus pluribus in locis asserit, decretum Dei & ejus voluntatem esse solam & unicam causam futuritionis cujuslibet eventus. Quid enim, An Dei decretum sola causa est cur Adam inobediens Deo futurus fuit: Et similiter cur Angeli illi qui ceciderunt, fuerunt adversus Deum superbia sese elaturi? Quis hoc dicentem audire sustineat? aut hoc dicere possit quin Deum peccati authorem manifeste faciat?
latin.2051: LVI. At, inquit, Doctus ille vir, futuritionis quae ab aeterno fuit nulla causa dari potest quae ab aeterno non fuerit. Nihil enim temporale causa est ejus quod ab aeterno est. Sed nihil ab aeterno fuit praeter Deum ipsum, qui non nisi per liberam suam voluntatem ad extra operatur. Respondeo, argumentum istud supponit futuritionem esse aliquid reale a re ipsa futura distinctum, & quod causam aliam habeat quam res ipsa futura. At hoc falsissimum est. Nam futuritio nihil aliud est quam respectus quidam rationis, & extrinseca denominatio rei quae futura dicitur: non vero ens aliquod a re futura distinctum, & quod requirat causam quandam diversam ab ipsius rei futurae causa. Et hoc patet ex ipso argumento. Nam recte ponit argumentum ab aeterno nihil fuisse praeter Deum: ac proinde futuritio quae ab aeterno fuisse dicitur, vel nihil reale fuit, vel fuit ipse Deus.
latin.2052: LVII. Igitur quod est causa cur res in tempore aliquando existat, idem plane causa est cur res ab aeterno extitura fuerit. Sicut quod causa est cur res aliquando fuit, causa est cur in aeternum dicetur praeterita. Nec magis requiritur causa ab aeterno existens, ut res ab aeterno futura fuerit, quam requiritur causa in aeternum duratura, ut in aeternum res praeterita sit. Ad effectum futurum sufficit causa futura, sicut ad praeteritum sufficit causa praeterita.
latin.2053: LVIII. Cum ergo Deus in tempore causa peccati non sit, tantum abest ut dicendum putem Dei voluntatem esse causam unicam futuritionis peccati, ut plane & simpliciter negandum existimem illam esse istius futuritionis causam, vel solam, vel cum causa secunda. Verum est quidem hominem non peccare, nisi dependenter a Dei voluntate. Nec enim peccare posset, nisi Deus ipsum peccare permitteret. Et sic quoque peccati futuritio pendet a decreto Dei de peccato permittendo. Sed quemadmodum Dei voluntas non propterea dicenda est propria causa cur homo actu peccet; sic etiam inde non sequitur Dei decretum esse propriam causam futuritionis peccati.
latin.2054: LIX. Sed etiam nonnulli eorum qui statuunt quosdam actus liberos absolute esse futuros, & ut tales a Deo praesciri, absque ullo decreto causas liberas ad istos actus praedeterminandi, ut Doctissimus Strangius; negant tamen futura contingentia libera a Deo cognosci posse ex ulla hypothesi quae non infert necessario determinationem voluntatis creatae, & proinde quae non includit absolutum decretum de eorum futuritione. Ut apud eundem Strangium videre est de Voluntate Dei circa peccatum, lib. 3. cap. 11.
latin.2055: LX. Ratio autem ejus est, ut supra retulimus, quod nihil certo cognosci potest quod non sit certo verum: nihil autem certo verum est quod necessarium non sit vel absolute, vel ex hypothesi. Unde colligit futura conditionata non posse esse objectum scientiae divinae, quae infallibilis & certissima est, nisi in conditione includatur aliquid unde quod dicitur futurum necessario inferatur. Sed si haec ratio valeret, nullum contingens Deus praescire posset tanquam absolute futurum, nisi quod prius absolute futurum decrevisset: quod tamen non admittit Strangius, qui fatetur homines multa libere agere ad quae a Deo non praedeterminantur.
latin.2056: LXI. Sed, ait vir ille Doctus, quicquid Deus praevidet ut absolute futurum, quantumlibet in se contingens sit, & simpliciter loquendo possit non esse, necessarium est tamen ex hypothesi, non quidem ex hypothesi divini alicujus decreti praedeterminantis, sed ex hac illa ipsa hypothesi quod futurum est. Etenim quemadmodum quicquid est, dum est, necessario est; ita etiam quicquid futurum est, hoc ipso quod supponitur futurum, necessario futurum est, & sic a Deo certo cognosci potest.
latin.2057: LXII. Sed quod vir Doctissimus de absolute futuris dicendum existimat, non minori cum ratione ad conditionate futura applicari potest. Dicam enim eodem modo Deum certo praevidere quod libere futurum esset sub aliqua conditione; quia licet causa libera posset aliter agere, nec ista conditio illi necessitatem agendi imponeret, nihilominus reipsa sic ageret. Ex hypothesi autem quod sic ageret, necesse est ut sic agat posita conditione, & ita res est quae possit a Deo certo sciri.
latin.2058: LXIII. Nihil ergo video cur negemus Deo scientiam eorum quae libere futura essent sub certa conditione, quanquam in conditione ista non includatur decretum de causa libera ad hoc vel illud praedeterminanda. Et si quae argumenta scientiam istam videntur evertere, ut quod capi non potest qua ratione Deus infallibiliter cognoscat futurum esse quod posset non esse, pugnant illa quoque cum praescientia contingentium quae sunt absolute futura; quam tamen in Deo dari verbum Dei ponit extra omne dubium.
latin.2059: LXIV. Sed certe tantum de nobis praesumere non debemus, ut divinam scientiam limitare ausimus, & negare quod Deus aliquid sciat, quia quomodo sciret comprehendere non valemus. Nam divinus intellectus omnimodo infinitus plus scit proculdubio quam valeamus capere & assequi. Saltem ille minus periculose errat, qui putat Deum scire ea quae forte scibilia non sunt; quam qui negat Deum scire quae revera scit, & quae intra divinae omniscientiae objectum continentur.
latin.2060: LXV. Addo scientiam illam futurorum conditionate, qualem hactenus descripsimus, nullam necessariam connexionem habere cum erroribus variis, ad quos tuendos atque incrustandos plurimi ea abutuntur. Praesertim vero pertendimus illam nullo modo pugnare cum gratia per se efficaci, neque necesse esse ut illam adhibeamus ad conciliandam divinae gratiae efficaciam cum arbitrii humani libertate. Ut in sequentibus, Deo favente, ostendemus.

sections.title: Voetius' disputants: two states of the object of God's knowledge but three moments; conditionals belong to free knowledge
sections.pass_a: XXXIII. And that those most learned men may explain their mind on that matter more distinctly, they say, That they consider in the object of divine knowledge two states, of possibility and of futurition, but three moments. The first, when God by beholding his omnipotence saw what could be done by himself without contradiction. The second, when he predefined with himself by an absolute decree the modes, connections, and concatenations of all things possible to be made, that is, what would be cause, what effect, what means, what end, what prior, what simultaneous, what posterior, or would not be; But with this caution, if he should will them to be future. The third, when among those things, predefined under such a condition, he set a difference, that condition being left to some, and such a decree being superadded, I will not that they be future, the condition being taken away from others, and in its place such a decree substituted, I will that they be future. That in the third moment the thing is at last drawn out of the state of possibility into the state of futurition: that in the two prior ones it remains in the state of possibility; yet with this difference, that he knows them in the first by nature, and before every act of the will, in the second after the act of the will. Which are also their words in that third section, num. 13. From which words it is clear that they hold future contingents under a condition not for truly future, but for merely possible, and yet will that their cognition pertain not to the natural knowledge of God, but to the free.
pass_b: To set out their view on the matter more distinctly, those very learned men say that in the object of God's knowledge they consider two states, possibility and futurity, but three moments. In the first, God, looking at his own omnipotence, saw what he could do without contradiction. In the second, by an absolute decree he fixed beforehand within himself the modes, connections and sequences of everything that could be made: what would or would not be cause, effect, means and end, what would come before, together or after. He did this with one proviso: if he willed them to be future.

In the third, among the things fixed beforehand under that condition, he made a distinction. For some he left the condition standing and added the decree 'I do not will them to be future.' For others he removed the condition and put in its place the decree 'I will them to be future.'

Only in the third moment, they say, is a thing finally brought out of the state of possibility into the state of futurity. In the first two it stays in the state of possibility. The difference is that God knows things in the first moment by nature, before any act of his will, and in the second after an act of his will. These too are their words, in that third section, number 13.

Their words make it plain that they treat contingent futures under a condition not as truly future but as merely possible. Yet they want the knowledge of them to belong not to God's natural knowledge but to his free knowledge.

sections.title: They take this from Samuel Rutherford: God's will is determined from eternity toward every being, so conditionals are true by his will
sections.pass_a: XXXIV. Whence they gather, that God necessarily wills, or does not will all the possible concatenations and connections of beings, and so in all conditional propositions concerning a future contingent, it is true from the definite and certain will of God, that if such or such a condition were posited, this and not another would follow.
pass_b: They admit that they took this doctrine from the Scot Samuel Rutherford, and in the same place they lay down, as a most certain foundation drawn from him, the following. God's will is not undetermined, doubtful or suspended toward any being, whether actual or potential, and whether it is to be actualized at some time or never brought into act.
Nor does his will contain potentiality, suspension and the lack of a second act, as a created will does. By the eminence of its act it is determined from eternity with respect to every being.

From this they infer that God necessarily wills or does not will every possible sequence and connection of beings. So in every conditional proposition about a contingent future, it is true by God's definite and certain will that if this or that condition were in place, this and nothing else would follow.

pass_b: Others, however, think that many, or rather countless, propositions about contingent futures under some condition can be framed and made up that do not fall under God's knowledge. They express nothing that God himself can know or understand.

This is not because God is ignorant of any truth, or because something is really future that God does not know to be future. It is because, in their view, such propositions signify nothing that is determinately true or false. What they affirm or deny as future under a certain condition is no more future than not future; it is open either way.

pass_b: Suppose someone says that if God created another world and placed certain angels in it in these or those circumstances, those angels would persevere in their duty and in the love of God. sections.title: They do not deny all knowledge of conditional futures, but derive it from absolute decrees about what really happens
sections.pass_a: XXXIX. Nor yet do they deny all knowledge in God of those things which would be, or would have been contingently future, under some condition, which has never been posited, nor is ever to be posited. For they acknowledge that certain things of that kind are foretold in scripture, and so were known and perceived by God. But they contend that that knowledge did not precede the free decree of the divine will. Not that they admit in God certain conditional decrees, by which he wills something to be done under a condition which will never take place: or also explicit and formal decrees concerning the connection of two events neither of which will actually exist: but because from certain absolute decrees of God concerning things really future it follows, such, or such a condition being posited, that these and those things would have been future.
pass_b: Even so, they do not deny that God has any knowledge of things that would be or would have been contingently future under a condition that has never been, and never will be, fulfilled. They grant that some things of this kind are foretold in Scripture and so were known to God and clearly seen by him. What they insist on is that this knowledge did not come before the free decree of God's will.

This is not because they allow in God conditional decrees, by which he wills something to happen under a condition that will never obtain. Nor do they allow explicit, formal decrees about the connection of two events, neither of which will actually exist. Their reason is that, given this or that condition, it follows from certain absolute decrees of God about things that will really happen that these or those things would have come about.

sections.title: Ames: an implicit, virtual decree grounds conditionals that never occur; they belong to the knowledge of vision
sections.pass_a: XLI. Thus William Ames explains that matter in his rescript to the Response of Grevinchoven, chap. 15. This also, he says, is worthy of careful contemplation: that the decree of God is conceived either as a formal and explicit statute, or as implicit and virtual, which is included by virtue of another decree: but that the implicit only is given in conditional future contingents, which never exist, because by virtue of actual decrees, this or that being posited, they would exist. pass_b: William Ames explains the matter this way in his rescript to Grevinchoven's Response, chapter 15. 'This too,' he says, 'deserves careful consideration. A decree of God may be conceived either as a formal and explicit statute, or as implicit and virtual, contained by the force of another decree. Only the implicit kind applies to conditional contingent futures that never come to exist, because by the force of actual decrees they would exist if this or that were posited.

God had decreed to free David from the men of Keilah by means of flight, not by changing their minds outside the usual order. From this actual decree flows the conditional contingent: if David does not flee, he will be handed over.'

sections.title: Their main foundation (Twisse): nothing is future before God decrees it, since futurity from eternity needs an eternal cause
sections.pass_a: XLII. Further the chief foundation on which Twisse, Rutherford, Voetius, Ames, and others rest, while they deny that there is given in God a cognition of things contingently future under some condition, before his free decree, is this, that, in their mind, Nothing is future before God has decreed it to be future. Whence it follows, that before the decree of God nothing can be conceived and known as future. But that nothing is either absolutely or conditionally future, before God decrees it to be future, they prove thence, that no cause can be feigned or thought, by which a thing from possible becomes future from eternity, besides the decree of God. For since nothing temporal can be the cause of that which is eternal, the cause of futurition, which is from eternity, ought to be referred to none of those things which are done in time, but it is necessary that that futurition have some eternal cause, which can be no other than the free decree of God: as Twisse repeats a thousand times in his dissertation on middle Knowledge.
pass_b: Twisse, Rutherford, Voetius, Ames and others deny that God knows, before his free decree, what would contingently happen under some condition. The main foundation they rely on is that, on their view, nothing is future until God has decreed that it shall be. It follows that before God's decree nothing can be conceived or known as future.

They prove that nothing is future, absolutely or conditionally, before God decrees it, on these grounds. No cause can be imagined or thought of, other than God's decree, by which a thing passes from being possible to being future from eternity. Nothing temporal can cause what is eternal.

So the futurity that exists from eternity cannot be traced to anything that happens in time. It must have some eternal cause, and that can only be God's free decree. Twisse repeats this a thousand times in his dissertation on middle knowledge.

sections.title: Voetius (Nethenus): the whole controversy turns on whether conditional futures can become future except by God's decree

This is the foundation of foundations, on which the whole weight of the cause rests; this is that postulate which both we cannot concede to the adversaries, and they cannot prove to us.
pass_b: Voetius, or rather Nethenus in Voetius's work, after arguing at length against middle knowledge, finally concludes: 'From what has been argued so far against middle knowledge, it is clear that the whole difficulty of the present controversy comes down to this point.

Could free conditional futures, which by their own nature are open to being future or not future, have passed from eternity into the state of something future in any way other than by the divine decree, which is the cause of every kind of futurity whatever? This is the foundation of foundations, on which the whole weight of the case rests. It is the postulate that we cannot grant our opponents and they cannot prove to us.'

sections.title: Strang's argument: conditionals without necessary connection cannot be known with certainty, so not by God
sections.pass_a: XLIV. But Strang, who does not think, with the Theologians just mentioned, that the futurition of any event from eternity depends on nothing else than the free decree of God, contends to prove by another argument, which he judges to be invincible, that free contingents cannot be known by God as future, from any hypothesis, from which the determination of the created will is not necessarily inferred. And his argument is such. Conditionals whose consequent has no necessary connection with the antecedent cannot be known with certainty, and therefore neither are they knowable by God, whose knowledge is most certain and altogether infallible. But of that kind are the conditionals which are stated to be the object of middle knowledge, &c. He proves the Major, because, he says, Unless the object be certainly true, it cannot be certainly known: for as long as the thing is uncertain, it cannot be certainly known; but nothing is certainly true which is not necessarily true, necessarily I say either absolutely, or by hypothesis. And therefore that conditional knowledge may be certain and infallible, its object must be a necessary conditional proposition: but no conditional proposition is necessary, in which the inference is not necessary. In the Treatise on the Will of God about sin book 3, chap. 11.
pass_b: Strang does not agree with the theologians just named that the futurity of every event from eternity depends on nothing but God's free decree. He tries to prove by another argument, which he considers unanswerable, that God cannot know free contingents as future on any supposition from which the determination of the created will does not necessarily follow.

His argument runs like this. Conditionals whose consequent has no necessary connection with the antecedent cannot be known with certainty, and so God cannot know them either, since his knowledge is entirely certain and infallible. The conditionals said to be the object of middle knowledge are of this kind, and so on.

He proves the major premise as follows: 'Unless the object is certainly true, it cannot be known with certainty. As long as the matter is uncertain, it cannot be known with certainty. But nothing is certainly true that is not necessarily true, necessarily, I mean, either absolutely or on a hypothesis.

So for conditional knowledge to be certain and infallible, its object must be a necessary conditional proposition. And no conditional proposition is necessary unless the inference in it is necessary.' Treatise on the Will of God concerning Sin, book 3, chapter 11.

Namely all propositions concerning conditional futures, that they may be able to be true, are to be so expounded and understood; this, or that creature set in such an order of things, will do this or that; provided God will to concur with it, as he is wont to concur, and as it is necessary that he concur in order that the creature may be able to elicit its action.
pass_b: To state briefly what I myself think: first, it is certain and, as is clear from what has been said, granted by everyone, that nothing is freely future under any condition, or can be known as such, unless God's decree not to deny the creature the concurrence necessary for acting is included in the condition under which it is said to be future.

That is, if any proposition about conditional futures is to be capable of truth, it must be explained and understood like this: this or that creature, placed in such an order of things, will do this or that, provided God wills to concur with it as he usually does. He must concur if the creature is to be able to put forth its action.

Secondly, I judge that this also is to be conceded, that all propositions concerning free and contingent conditional futures, in which a condition of that kind is understood, are determinately true or false. At least this the more recent Thomists cannot deny, and others who think with them in this business, and otherwise most sharply impugn middle Knowledge. For since in order that the creature act, according to their opinion, it is necessary that God premove and predetermine it, and God's predetermination being posited, the action of the creature necessarily follows, according to their hypotheses this conditional is infallible and necessary, If God willed to set such a creature in this, or that state, and to deny it nothing necessary for acting, it would do this or that: since in that condition is contained the decree of God concerning predetermining it to act.
pass_b: Second, I think it must also be granted that every proposition about free and contingent conditional futures, where a condition of that kind is understood, is determinately true or false. At any rate the later Thomists cannot deny this, nor can others who agree with them on this matter while otherwise attacking middle knowledge fiercely.

On their view, for a creature to act God must premove and predetermine it, and once God's predetermination is posited the creature's action follows necessarily. So on their assumptions this conditional is infallible and necessary: if God willed to place such a creature in this or that state and to deny it nothing it needs to act, it would do this or that. For that condition contains God's decree to predetermine the creature to act.

sections.title: The reasons for determinate truth in absolute future propositions hold for these conditionals too
sections.pass_a: XLVII. And certainly the reasons which persuade that absolute propositions concerning future contingents have determinate truth, or falsity, seem to have place also in these conditionals. Namely that it cannot be, but that of two contradictories, one is true, the other false. Likewise that in every true disjunctive, one part at least must be true. For this disjunctive is true, If Peter be set in such an occasion, and God deny him not his wonted concurrence, he will sin, or will not sin. And these two also mutually contradict each other, Peter if he be placed in that order of things, and God be not unwilling to concur with him for acting, will do this. And Peter if he be placed in that order of things, and God be not unwilling to concur with him for acting, will not do this.
pass_b: The reasons that lead us to hold that absolute propositions about contingent futures are determinately true or false seem to apply to these conditionals as well. One is that of two contradictories one must be true and the other false. Another is that in every true disjunction at least one part must be true.

For this disjunction is true: if Peter is placed in such an occasion and God does not deny him his usual concurrence, he will sin or he will not sin. But for a thing not to be simply future, only future under some condition, no decree actually present in God is needed. sections.pass_a: LI. Nor is it less evident, according to the principles of the same Doctors, that that knowledge by which God knows what any possible creature would do in this or that state of things, if God willed to supply to it the concurrence necessary for acting, has place in God in reason before he has decreed anything concerning things. sections.title: A prior decree fixing all connections of possibles is fiction, idle, and unworthy of God's goodness and justice
sections.pass_a: LII. Nay also that decree seems plainly fictitious, and repugnant not only to wisdom, but also to the divine goodness, by which some will, as we related above, that God predefined with himself the connections and concatenations of all things possible to be made, before he decreed anything to be future. For if it were so, it would be necessary that God, before he resolved to create this world, should have conceived with himself decrees of this kind, if I will to create Adam, I will that his fall cohere necessarily with his temptation. If I will to create David and him to see Bathsheba, I will that with that sight be connected the concupiscence of that woman. Likewise, I will that such occasions of sinning be followed by such sins, if I decree that such occasions shall be. Nay I will that in infinite worlds creatable by me these and those events contingently possible have an inseparable nexus with these and those events of the same nature. Which decrees certainly are not only plainly idle, frivolous and vain, but most greatly misbecome the goodness and justice of him who is a God not willing iniquity.
pass_b: Indeed, the decree some posit, as reported above, by which God fixed within himself the connections and sequences of everything that could be made before he decreed anything to be future, seems pure invention. It seems contrary not only to God's wisdom but also to his goodness.

If it were so, God would have had to form decrees like these within himself before resolving to create this world: 'If I will to create Adam, I will that his fall be necessarily bound up with his temptation. If I will to create David and that he see Bathsheba, I will that lust for that woman be joined to that sight.'

Or again: 'I will that such occasions of sin be followed by such sins, if I decree that such occasions shall exist.' Or even: 'I will that in the countless worlds I could create, these or those contingently possible events be inseparably linked with these or those events of the same kind.'

It cannot therefore be denied with any reason, and ought to be conceded by all, that there is given in God a certain knowledge of those things which are freely and contingently future, under a certain condition, before we conceive any actual decree concerning future things in God. The whole difficulty is Whether the condition under which a thing is said to be future ought to include a decree concerning premoving and predetermining the second cause to act, or whether it suffices that the decree, which according to that condition would have to be posited in God, be only concerning affording a certain concurrence indifferent of itself, and which is determined by the second cause to a certain species of action.
pass_b: So it cannot reasonably be denied, and everyone ought to grant, that God has a certain knowledge of what is freely and contingently future under a certain condition, before we conceive of any actual decree in God about future things.

The whole difficulty is this. Must the condition under which something is said to be future include a decree to premove and predetermine the second cause to act? Or is it enough that the decree which that condition would require in God be simply a decree to provide a concurrence that is of itself indifferent and is determined by the second cause to a particular kind of action?

sections.title: Predeterminists require a predetermining decree in the condition; Le Blanc denies predetermination to evil acts lest God author sin
sections.pass_a: LIV. All those Theologians who think that nothing is done without the concurrence of God applying and predetermining the second cause to act, contend that no proposition concerning contingent and conditional futures has any truth, and so is knowable as true, unless in the condition there be supposed a decree concerning premoving and predetermining the free agent. For they will that the futurition of any action whatever depends on such a decree, nay according to some, as on a cause sole and solitary, and that without such a decree no action of a second cause can be future. But we are of the opinion that second causes do many things in time to which they are not predetermined by God. For we do not see how God would not be the author of sin, if he predetermined free causes to acts by themselves vicious and intrinsically evil, for example to blasphemy, and to the hatred of God. But if some action of a free cause can be without the premotion and predetermination of God, in order that some action be future, or would be future, it is not necessary that there be posited, or supposed in God a decree concerning premoving and predetermining the creature to act: but there suffices a decree concerning affording that concurrence, without which the creature can do nothing, and which is truly necessary to its action.
pass_b: All the theologians who think nothing happens without God's concurrence applying and predetermining the second cause to act insist that no proposition about contingent conditional futures has any truth, or can be known as true, unless a decree to premove and predetermine the free agent is assumed in the condition.
They hold that the futurity of every action depends on such a decree, and some even make it the sole and only cause. Without such a decree, they say, no action of a second cause can be future.

Our view, however, is that second causes do many things in time to which God does not predetermine them. We do not see how God would escape being the author of sin if he predetermined free causes to acts that are vicious in themselves and intrinsically evil, such as blasphemy and hatred of God.

But if a free cause can perform some action without God's premotion and predetermination, then for an action to be future, or to be such that it would be future, there is no need to posit or suppose in God a decree to premove and predetermine the creature to act. A decree to provide the concurrence without which the creature can do nothing, and which its action really needs, is enough.

sections.title: Twisse's argument from eternal futurity; reply: futurity is only a relation of reason, an extrinsic denomination
sections.pass_a: LVI. But, says that learned man, of the futurition which was from eternity no cause can be given which was not from eternity. For nothing temporal is the cause of that which is from eternity. But nothing was from eternity besides God himself, who does not operate outwardly except through his free will. I answer, that argument supposes futurition to be something real distinct from the future thing itself, and which has another cause than the future thing itself. But this is most false. For futurition is nothing else than a certain respect of reason, and an extrinsic denomination of the thing which is said to be future: but not some being distinct from the future thing, and which requires some cause diverse from the cause of the future thing itself. And this is clear from the argument itself. For the argument rightly posits that from eternity nothing was besides God: and therefore the futurition which is said to have been from eternity, either was nothing real, or was God himself.
pass_b: 'But,' says that learned man, 'no cause can be given for a futurity that existed from eternity unless the cause itself existed from eternity. Nothing temporal causes what exists from eternity. But nothing existed from eternity except God himself, who acts outside himself only through his free will.'

My answer is that this argument assumes that futurity is something real, distinct from the future thing itself and having a cause other than that thing. That is entirely false. Futurity is nothing but a certain relation of reason, an extrinsic denomination of the thing said to be future. It is not some being distinct from the future thing that needs a cause different from the cause of the future thing itself.
The argument itself makes this plain. It rightly assumes that nothing existed from eternity except God. So the futurity said to have existed from eternity was either nothing real or God himself.

sections.pass_a: LVII. Therefore that which is the cause why a thing at some time exists in time, the same plainly is the cause why the thing from eternity was going to exist. For a future effect a future cause suffices, as for a past one a past cause suffices.

A cause existing from eternity is no more needed for a thing to have been future from eternity than a cause lasting for ever is needed for a thing to be past for ever. A future cause is enough for a future effect, just as a past cause is enough for a past one.

sections.pass_a: LVIII. Since therefore God is not the cause of sin in time, so far am I from thinking it should be said that the will of God is the only cause of the futurition of sin, that I judge it must plainly & simply be denied that it is the cause of that futurition, either alone, or with the second cause. It is true indeed that man does not sin, except dependently on the will of God. For he could not sin, unless God permitted him to sin. And thus also the futurition of sin depends on the decree of God concerning permitting sin. But just as the will of God is not on that account to be called the proper cause why man actually sins; so also it does not follow thence that the decree of God is the proper cause of the futurition of sin.
pass_b: Since God is not the cause of sin in time, I am far from thinking we should say that God's will is the only cause of sin's futurity. On the contrary, I judge that we must deny plainly and without qualification that it is the cause of that futurity at all, whether on its own or together with the second cause.
It is true that man sins only in dependence on God's will, since he could not sin unless God permitted him to. In that sense the futurity of sin also depends on God's decree to permit sin.
But God's will is not for that reason to be called the proper cause of man's actually sinning. In the same way, it does not follow that God's decree is the proper cause of the futurity of sin.

sections.title: We must not limit God's knowledge because we cannot grasp how he knows; it is safer to err on the side of his knowing
sections.pass_a: LXIV. But certainly we ought not to presume so much of ourselves, that we dare to limit the divine knowledge, & to deny that God knows something, because we are not able to comprehend how he would know it. For the divine intellect infinite in every mode knows without doubt more than we are able to grasp & attain. At least he errs less dangerously, who thinks that God knows those things which perhaps are not knowable; than he who denies that God knows the things which he truly knows, & which are contained within the object of the divine omniscience.
pass_b: We certainly ought not to presume so much on ourselves as to dare to set limits to God's knowledge and deny that he knows something because we cannot understand how he would know it. God's intellect, infinite in every way, doubtless knows more than we can grasp or reach.

At any rate, someone who thinks God knows things that perhaps are not knowable errs less dangerously than someone who denies that God knows what he really does know, things that fall within the object of his omniscience.

sections.title: Conditional knowledge has no necessary tie to the errors it is used to defend, nor to reconciling efficacious grace with freedom
sections.pass_a: LXV. I add that that knowledge of conditional futures, such as we have hitherto described, has no necessary connection with various errors, to defend & varnish which very many abuse it. But especially we contend that it in no way fights with grace efficacious by itself, nor is it necessary that we employ it to reconcile the efficacy of divine grace with the liberty of human choice. As in what follows, God favouring, we shall show.
pass_b: I add that the knowledge of conditional futures, as described so far, has no necessary connection with the various errors that very many misuse it to defend and gloss over.

Above all, we maintain that it in no way conflicts with grace that is efficacious of itself, and that we do not need it to reconcile the efficacy of God's grace with the freedom of human choice. With God's help, we will show this in what follows.
